subject: History of Pakistan & India
title: 9. Democracy, Political Parties and Constitutional Politics in Pakistan

segments.text: This topic asks candidates to evaluate, not merely narrate, the quality of Pakistan’s democratic experience. A list of prime ministers and election dates, however accurate, answers a different and much weaker question than the one usually asked: has elected government in Pakistan become institutionally stable, and if not, why not? This topic pulls together threads from Topics 6 and 7 (constitutional structure and military intervention) and applies them specifically to the record of party politics and elections since 1947.

As Topic 6 explained in detail, Pakistan’s first parliamentary experiment suffered from constitutional delay, weak party organisation, and growing bureaucratic and gubernatorial intervention in political processes, ending with the 1958 military takeover before the country had held a single general election under its own completed constitution. This period is best treated in this topic as the baseline against which every later phase of Pakistani democracy should be measured — not as a fully separate story, since its causes (institutional imbalance, weak parties) are the same structural causes examined at length in Topic 7.

Zulfikar Ali Bhutto’s government, formed after the 1971 crisis (Topic 8) and operating under the newly adopted 1973 Constitution (Topic 6), restored parliamentary, civilian-led politics after over a decade of military and quasi-military rule. Bhutto’s Pakistan People’s Party pursued a broadly populist and left-leaning domestic programme, including nationalisation of major industries, banks and educational institutions, alongside land reforms aimed at reducing large landholdings. At the same time, Bhutto’s period was also marked by increasing political centralisation, harsh treatment of political opposition in several instances, and growing controversy — most consequentially, allegations of large-scale rigging in the March 1977 general election, which the Pakistan National Alliance (an opposition coalition) rejected, launching a sustained protest movement that created the political crisis General Zia-ul-Haq’s July 1977 coup (Topic 7) then exploited to remove Bhutto’s government entirely. Bhutto was subsequently tried and, controversially, executed in 1979 following a murder conviction that many observers, then and since, have regarded as politically motivated — itself a further illustration of how thoroughly institutional and judicial processes could become entangled with military-political power during this period.

blocks.text: Democratic Revival, 1988–1999: A Decade of Alternation and Dismissal

segments.text: Following Zia’s death in 1988, Pakistan returned to an eleven-year period of elected civilian government — but one marked by remarkable political instability, with
no elected government completing its full constitutional term
during this entire period. Benazir Bhutto (Pakistan People’s Party) and Nawaz Sharif (Pakistan Muslim League-N) alternated in office, each serving two non-consecutive terms:

items.text: Benazir Bhutto became prime minister in 1988 (the first woman to lead the government of a Muslim-majority country) but was dismissed by President Ghulam Ishaq Khan in 1990 using the Eighth Amendment’s Article 58(2)(b) dissolution power (Topic 6), amid allegations of corruption and mismanagement.

Nawaz Sharif’s first government (1990–1993) was similarly dismissed by presidential order, though the dismissal was briefly reversed by the Supreme Court before Sharif ultimately agreed to resign amid continuing political and civil-military tension.

Benazir Bhutto’s second government (1993–1996) was dismissed by President Farooq Leghari in 1996, again invoking Article 58(2)(b), amid corruption allegations and the controversial extrajudicial killing of her brother Murtaza Bhutto.

Nawaz Sharif’s second government (1997–1999), elected with a strong parliamentary majority that allowed him to pass the Thirteenth Amendment repealing Article 58(2)(b) (Topic 6), was ultimately removed not by presidential dismissal but by General Musharraf’s October 1999 military coup (Topic 7), following the Kargil conflict crisis and Sharif’s attempt to dismiss Musharraf as army chief.

segments.text: This decade illustrates a recurring pattern worth stating explicitly: repeated presidential dismissals under Article 58(2)(b), civil-military tension, and unstable party competition together prevented any single elected government from consolidating power over a full term, even though regular elections were, in a narrow sense, being held throughout the period — an important reminder that holding elections and achieving democratic consolidation are related but distinct achievements.

blocks.text: The Post-2008 Parliamentary Era: Greater Continuity, Continuing Strain

segments.text: Following Musharraf’s resignation in 2008 (Topic 7), Pakistan entered a period of markedly greater, though still imperfect, constitutional continuity:

items.text: The
2008 election

, held shortly after the assassination of Benazir Bhutto in December 2007, brought the Pakistan People’s Party (under Asif Ali Zardari) to government in coalition, and this government became the first in Pakistan’s history to complete a full five-year constitutional term.
The
Eighteenth Amendment (2010)

(Topic 6), reducing presidential power and substantially expanding provincial autonomy, is widely regarded as a landmark achievement of this parliament, reflecting a rare degree of cross-party consensus on strengthening parliamentary and provincial institutions.
The
2013 election

produced Pakistan’s first-ever transfer of power from one democratically elected civilian government that had completed a full term (the PPP) to another elected civilian government (Nawaz Sharif’s PML-N) — a genuine institutional milestone, even though Sharif’s own government was later removed from office in 2017 following a Supreme Court disqualification arising from the “Panama Papers” corruption investigation, rather than completing its own full term without incident.
The
2018 election
brought Imran Khan and his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party to power. Khan’s government was removed in
April 2022

through a successful parliamentary vote of no confidence — itself a notable, if contested, institutional event, since it marked the first time in Pakistan’s history that a sitting prime minister was removed through this specific parliamentary mechanism rather than through presidential dismissal, judicial disqualification, or military intervention. Khan and his supporters characterised the vote as the product of external and military interference; his opponents characterised it as a legitimate exercise of parliamentary accountability following the loss of his governing coalition’s majority. Both characterisations remain part of an active and contested political debate in Pakistan rather than a matter on which this resource should take a side.
Shehbaz Sharif led a coalition government from April 2022 until the
2024 general election

, after which he was elected prime minister by the National Assembly on 3 March 2024, again as the head of a coalition government. The conduct and outcome of the 2024 election, including the treatment of PTI-affiliated candidates who contested as independents, remained a subject of significant domestic political dispute and international commentary; candidates preparing very recent material should consult current, dated sources rather than relying on any single characterisation as settled historical fact, given how recent and contested this period remains.

blocks.text: Political Parties: Structure and Persistent Weaknesses

segments.text: Pakistan’s major political parties mobilise voters, aggregate and represent regional and social interests, and connect society to the state — the core functions any democracy requires of its party system. At the same time, several structural weaknesses recur across the party system as a whole and are frequently the subject of exam questions asking candidates to “evaluate” rather than simply describe Pakistani democracy:

items.text: Dynastic leadership.

Pakistan’s two largest and most historically durable parties have both been led, for most of their history, by members of a single founding family — the Bhutto family in the Pakistan People’s Party, and the Sharif family in the Pakistan Muslim League-N — raising persistent questions about internal party democracy and leadership succession.
Patronage networks and weak local organisation.

Candidate selection in many parties has often depended heavily on local patronage networks (particularly influential landowning or “electable” local notables) rather than on programmatic party membership or grassroots organisational structures, weakening parties’ ability to enforce internal discipline or maintain consistent policy positions between elections.
Regional and ethnic parties.

Beyond the two dominant national parties, regionally based parties — the Muttahida Qaumi Movement in urban Sindh (particularly Karachi), the Awami National Party in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and various nationalist parties in Balochistan and interior Sindh — play a significant role in provincial politics and in shaping federal coalition arithmetic, reflecting Pakistan’s real ethnic and regional diversity in ways the two dominant national parties do not fully capture on their own.

segments.text: A complete evaluation of Pakistani democracy has to look beyond the electoral cycle itself to the surrounding institutional environment:

items.text: The judiciary

became a significantly more assertive institutional actor from the mid-2000s onward, especially following the 2007 lawyers’ movement in defence of judicial independence (Topic 7) and a subsequent period of expanded judicial activism, including high-profile disqualifications of sitting prime ministers — a development some analysts view as a welcome check on executive impunity, and others view as a form of unelected institutional overreach into matters more appropriately settled through the electoral process.
The Election Commission of Pakistan’s

independence and administrative capacity has been a recurring subject of political dispute across virtually every recent election cycle, with losing parties frequently alleging irregularities and the Commission’s own institutional strengthening (partly addressed by the Eighteenth Amendment’s revised appointment mechanism) remaining an area of ongoing political negotiation.
The military’s continuing informal influence

over major national-security and, at times, broader political questions, discussed at length in Topic 7, means that formal electoral outcomes do not by themselves fully determine the practical distribution of power — an important qualification to any answer that measures democratic quality by election results alone.

blocks.text: How to Judge Democratic Quality: A Framework, Not a Checklist

segments.text: Political scientists generally evaluate democratic quality along several distinct dimensions rather than a single yes/no criterion: the fairness and competitiveness of elections; the degree of constitutional continuity and predictable, peaceful transfer of power; the strength and independence of parliament relative to the executive and other unelected institutions; the protection of civil liberties and rights; the degree of genuine internal democracy and programmatic coherence within political parties; the functioning of federalism and centre-province relations; and the quality of governance outcomes actually delivered to citizens. Applying this multi-dimensional framework to Pakistan’s post-2008 record produces a genuinely mixed picture — meaningful gains in constitutional continuity and civilian-to-civilian transfers of power, alongside continuing weaknesses in party institutionalisation, judicial-executive balance, and the military’s informal influence — and a strong exam answer should reflect this mixed picture rather than reaching for either an uncritically positive or uncritically negative single verdict.

items.text: Article 58(2)(b):

The Eighth Amendment provision used to dismiss three elected governments during the 1988–1999 period before its repeal (1997) and later, differently framed, partial restoration (2003) and permanent removal (2010) — see Topic 6.
Panama Papers case:
The 2016–2017 investigation and subsequent Supreme Court disqualification of Nawaz Sharif from office, an important instance of judicial-executive interaction in this period.
Vote of no confidence (2022):
The parliamentary procedure used to remove Prime Minister Imran Khan in April 2022, the first successful use of this specific mechanism against a sitting Pakistani prime minister.
Dynastic party leadership:
The pattern, common to Pakistan’s two largest parties, of leadership concentrated within a single founding family across multiple generations.

Prepare democratic periods as labelled phases (1947–58; 1971–77; 1988–99; 2008–present) rather than as an undifferentiated list of prime ministers, and for each phase ask: what did elections change, how strong were parliament and parties, what role did the presidency, judiciary or military play, and what constitutional reforms occurred?
Prepare the 1988–1999 period specifically as a case study in “elections without consolidation,” using the four dismissals as your core evidence.

Prepare the post-2008 period as a case study in gradual, still-incomplete consolidation, citing the 2013 civilian-to-civilian transfer and the Eighteenth Amendment as the strongest positive evidence, and the 2022 no-confidence vote and continuing judicial-executive tension as evidence of continuing strain.

Keep an evidence bank: the 1977 election crisis and Bhutto’s execution (1979), the four dismissals of 1990–1999, the 2008 and 2013 elections, the Eighteenth Amendment (2010), the Panama Papers disqualification (2017), and the 2022 no-confidence vote.
Practice one analytical outline answering: “Has Pakistani democracy become more institutionally stable since 2008? Use evidence for and against before reaching a judgment.”

Do not use “democracy” as a synonym for elections alone; apply the multi-dimensional framework (constitutional continuity, party institutionalisation, judicial-executive balance, civil liberties, federalism, governance outcomes) set out above.
Do not write a list of prime ministers without evaluating institutions and constitutional change; examiners specifically reward evaluative structure over narrative listing on this topic.

Do not assume every transfer of power is equally democratic in character; carefully distinguish elections, parliamentary votes of no confidence, presidential dismissals, judicial disqualifications, and military interventions from one another.

Do not take a partisan position on contested recent events (such as the circumstances of the 2022 no-confidence vote or the 2024 election); present the competing characterisations fairly and note that they remain actively disputed.

Pakistan experienced repeated interruptions of elected civilian rule between 1947 and 2008, making democratic consolidation a long-term institutional challenge rather than a single achieved milestone.
No elected government completed a full constitutional term during the 1988–1999 period; all four governments were dismissed or removed before completing their terms.
The Eighteenth Constitutional Amendment of 2010 strengthened parliamentary arrangements and substantially expanded provincial autonomy.
The 2013 election produced Pakistan’s first transfer of power from one elected civilian government completing a full term to another elected civilian government.
Imran Khan became prime minister after the 2018 election and was removed through a parliamentary vote of no confidence in April 2022, the first successful use of this mechanism in Pakistan’s history.

Following the 2024 general election, Shehbaz Sharif was elected prime minister by the National Assembly on 3 March 2024; the conduct of this election remained a subject of significant domestic and international dispute.

Evaluating Pakistani democracy requires a multi-dimensional framework — elections, constitutional continuity, party institutionalisation, judicial-executive balance, civil liberties, federalism, and governance outcomes — rather than treating regular elections alone as sufficient evidence of democratic consolidation.

The 1988–1999 period is best understood as a case study in “elections without consolidation”: regular elections occurred, but no government completed a full term, largely due to the interaction of Article 58(2)(b), civil-military tension, and unstable party competition.

The post-2008 period shows genuine, if incomplete, progress toward constitutional continuity — most clearly demonstrated by the 2013 civilian-to-civilian transfer of power and the consensus-based Eighteenth Amendment — alongside continuing strain from judicial-executive tension, contested elections, and the military’s informal influence.

Pakistan’s major parties remain marked by dynastic leadership and patronage-based organisation, a structural weakness distinct from, but related to, the institutional instability examined elsewhere in this topic and in Topic 7.

Recent and highly contested events (the 2022 no-confidence vote, the 2024 election) should be presented with both sides of the political dispute fairly represented, since they remain live, actively contested matters rather than settled historical fact.
